In early modern Europe, double-entry bookkeeping was associated with theological and cosmological concepts, such as the scales of justice and the symmetry of God's world.

The earliest known records of this system in Europe date to the "13th century", created by the Florentine merchant Amatino Manucci. The Farolfi firm's ledger from "1299–1300" provides evidence of this method in practice.

Today, the fundamental accounting equation defines the relationship between debits and credits across five specific categories: assets, capital, liabilities, revenues, and expenses. Every financial transaction involves two equal and opposite effects known as debit and credit.

Luca Pacioli is frequently referred to as the father of accounting because he was the first to publish a detailed description of the double-entry system. 

Accounting practices vary globally, with systems like Desi Namu originating from India and Merdiban serving as an accounting framework for the Ottoman Empire.
bodies.thread:
In early modern Europe, double-entry bookkeeping was associated with theological concepts, specifically the scales of justice and the symmetry of God's world.

The earliest known records of this system in Europe date to the 13th century, created by the Florentine merchant Amatino Manucci.

Evidence of complete double-entry bookkeeping appears in the Farolfi firm's ledger from 1299–1300.

Luca Pacioli is frequently referred to as the father of accounting because he was the first to publish a detailed description of the system.

The method requires that every transaction be recorded with equal and opposite debits and credits to ensure the books remain balanced.

By convention, debit entries are placed on the left side of a ledger account, while credit entries are placed on the right.

The fundamental accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity defines the relationship between these debits and credits.

Double-entry bookkeeping is a rigorous, historically established method for ensuring financial accuracy by recording every transaction as both a debit and a credit.
